planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into well-drained, average, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Chiapas sage roots to the ground in hard freezes but reliably resprouts from the base in zone 8–9 gardens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Chiapas sage is a compact, mounding Mexican salvia with small, glossy, dark green leaves and slender spikes of vivid magenta-pink flowers produced almost continuously from spring through the first hard frost, with the heaviest flush in fall. Its dense, tidy habit and long bloom season make it a reliable filler for borders and large containers, and hummingbirds visit it steadily throughout the warm months. In zone 8, expect the top growth to die back in a hard freeze, with new shoots emerging from the crown once the soil warms in spring; a layer of mulch over the root zone improves winter survival at the cold edge of its range. Cut plants back by about a third in late winter to encourage bushy new growth and the season's heaviest bloom.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade, giving this large Mexican highland sage plenty of room to reach full size before blooming in fall.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade with room to grow into a large, upright shrub; Mexican scarlet sage produces some of the largest, most dramatic flowers of any commonly grown salvia, with brilliant orange-red tubular blooms emerging from near-black calyces on tall spikes that appear from late summer into fall. It is a late-season showstopper and one of the most reliable hummingbird magnets available for a fall garden, drawing migrating hummingbirds heavily as they pass through in September and October. Because it flowers so late in the year, an early hard freeze in the northern part of its range can cut the display short, so site it in a warm, sheltered spot at the cold edge of its hardiness. Pinch young plants once or twice in early summer to encourage bushier growth and more flowering stems, and cut back to the base after a killing frost, mulching well over winter.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; this fast-growing Mexican sage benefits from a full growing season to reach flowering size before fall bloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Baja fireworks sage grows quickly into a large, upright shrub with soft, velvety, gray-green leaves and dense spikes of rich rose-magenta to fuchsia flowers that open over an extended fall display, often continuing until the first hard frost. Its rapid growth rate and heavy fall bloom make it a favorite for adding late-season color and hummingbird activity when many other perennials have finished flowering. Give it full sun for the most compact, floriferous growth, though it also performs well with afternoon shade in the hottest climates. Cut the woody framework back hard after a killing frost and mulch the crown, since new growth from the base each spring produces the strongest, most floriferous stems for the coming season.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings well after last frost into rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Wagner's sage is a large, understory Central American salvia more cold-sensitive than most other tender sages and needs a sheltered site at the cold edge of its zone range.

directions: Plant in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Wagner's sage is a large, coarse-textured Central American salvia with broad, bold leaves and dramatic winter to early-spring flower spikes wrapped in showy, rose-pink to mauve bracts that persist attractively even as the small white and pink flowers inside them fade. Its understory origin in humid mountain forests makes it more tolerant of shade and humidity than many other tender salvias, and it performs best with protection from hot, direct afternoon sun and from drying wind. Because it is among the more cold-sensitive of the commonly grown tender sages, plant it in a sheltered microclimate in zone 9, and expect significant dieback or loss in a hard freeze without heavy mulching over the crown. Where winter cold is a concern, growing a potted specimen that can be moved under cover is a safer option than relying on in-ground survival.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts in spring into very well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; chuparosa is a Sonoran and Mojave Desert wash-dweller adapted to intense heat, drought, and poor soil.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, sandy soil in full sun; chuparosa is a sprawling, nearly leafless desert shrub of the American Southwest with slender gray-green stems that carry out most of the plant's photosynthesis, an adaptation to extreme drought and heat in its native washes and rocky desert flats. Tubular, bright red-orange flowers, rich in nectar, are produced heavily in late winter and spring and again after summer rains, and are one of the most reliable early-season hummingbird nectar sources in the low desert, giving the plant its Spanish common name meaning 'hummingbird sipper.' It tolerates reflected heat, poor rocky soil, and long dry spells that would kill most other flowering shrubs, needing supplemental water only to establish and during the driest extended stretches. Prune out dead or frost-damaged wood in spring, since plants may drop leaves or die back partially in a hard freeze but generally resprout well from older wood.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after last frost into rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Brazilian red cloak is a fast-growing tropical shrub best treated as a large container specimen or root-hardy perennial outside true frost-free zones.

directions: Plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Brazilian red cloak is a bold, fast-growing tropical shrub grown for its striking upright flower spikes, in which large, deep red-maroon bracts overlap like shingles and part to reveal pure white, tubular flowers, creating a strong color contrast that blooms heavily from late summer into winter in frost-free climates. Large, glossy, dark green leaves give the shrub a lush, substantial presence even between flowering flushes, quickly filling out a tropical border or privacy planting where winters stay mild. It grows rapidly and can become leggy without regular pinching or a hard pruning in early spring, which encourages the dense, well-branched form that shows off the flower spikes best. Where frost is a risk, grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter, or mulch heavily and expect it to die back and resprout from the roots after a light freeze.
